name: qdmr
desc: Codeplug programming tool for DMR radios
why: Programs DMR radio codeplugs over USB; a real door into amateur radio hardware and its odd file formats.

brief.what_it_is: qdmr is a free, GPL-3.0 licensed GUI and command-line tool for building and writing 'codeplugs', the configuration files that program DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) handsets. You assemble channels, zones, contacts, RX groups, scan lists, radio ID, and APRS/GPS settings for a supported radio, and it uploads them to the device, with downloads from the radio supported too. The stored result is a human-readable text file rather than a vendor binary, so it can be shared between devices. The GUI can pull nearby repeater frequencies from repeatermap.de and fetch the DMR call-sign database for contact auto-completion. The page names a command-line tool, dmrconf, which ships with a man page.
brief.why_it_exists: The author says vendor DMR programming software for cheap radios is hard to use, poorly documented, often Windows-only, and produces device-specific binaries that cannot be shared, so amateur operators must redo regional setup for every model. qdmr is meant to cut the feature set to what amateur use needs and make setup friendlier.
brief.how_it_works: Codeplugs are stored as a device-independent human-readable text file, and the tool converts that to each supported radio's own format for upload. The page says it is derived from Serge KK6ABQ's reverse-engineering of cheap Chinese DMR radio code-plug formats and communication protocols, reworked for interactive use. Repeater and call-sign lookups come from repeatermap.de (which requires an API key from its maintainer) and a downloaded DMR ID database.
brief.install_notes: The page says there are several install routes, from App-package downloads to building from source, and points to a separate install instructions page that I did not fetch. Building requires Qt6, since the page links Qt6 API docs for the GUI and command-line tools. Repeater auto-completion needs a repeatermap.de API key requested from Martin DK3ML, and location lookup uses the locator set in the settings dialog or the OS location service. Radios are connected over USB serial, which the 0.6.2 release note mentions for MacOS 11.
brief.standout: Instead of a binary blob, the codeplug is a plain text file that works across models and vendors, which makes sharing and diffing configs practical. The GUI also pulls real repeater frequencies and the DMR call-sign database, so contacts can be added by callsign instead of numeric DMR ID.
brief.status: Maintained, based on the page: the version history runs through 0.15.0 (adds AnyTone AT-D168UV), there are regular bugfix releases, and the license notice covers 2019-2026. The page gives no release dates or commit dates, so the exact recency is unknown.
brief.caveats: Only a small set of radios is supported. The author owns just three (Radioddity/Baofeng RD-5R, Retevis RT3S, AnyTone AT-D878UV), and support for the rest comes from reports and testers. Features are deliberately reduced to amateur use, and Serge's dmrconfig supports more models. The support table marks the Baofeng DR-1801-A6 with 'Stay away!', and the 0.9.0-alpha3 release was an alpha after a core rewrite that may have added bugs. The version list repeats 0.12.3 twice and the license line calls it a 'GUI programming tool for Chinese DMR radios', which does not quite match the tagline. Some features (APRS, GPS, call-sign DB upload) only work on radios that support them. The page's own text mentions that DMR encryption is illegal for ham use, but does not describe how the tool handles it.
quotes: A codeplug programming tool for DMR radios

it does not store the final code-plug in a device-specific binary format, but in a human-readable text file that is device independent and can therefore be shared across multiple device and even across vendors
Since I only own three DMR radios a Radioddity/Baofeng RD-5R, a Retevis RT3S and an AnyTone AT-D878UV, only a few radios are supported right now
